questions.question: What are the five prerequisites that must be in place before running chaos experiments in production?
options: Load testing, canary deployment, feature flags, blue-green routing, rollback scripts
Defined SLI/SLO, trace+metric+log observability, automated rollback, runbooks, on-call
Code review, security audit, performance baseline, staging test, stakeholder approval
Container scanning, SBOM, vulnerability patching, firewall rules, WAF configuration
questions.explanation: The five prerequisites: defined SLI/SLO (so you know what normal looks like), full observability (traces + metrics + logs to detect impact), automated rollback (to exit experiments instantly), runbooks (to handle discovered failures), and on-call (a human in the loop during experiments).

questions.question: What is the burn-rate guardrail that automatically pauses a chaos experiment?
options: Pause if P99 TTFT exceeds 2x the SLO value
Pause if daily error-budget burn exceeds 2x expected
Pause if GPU utilization drops below 50%
Pause if the experiment has been running more than 1 hour
questions.explanation: The lesson's mandatory guardrail: burn-rate alerts pause experiments automatically if the daily error-budget burn exceeds 2x the expected rate. This prevents an experiment from consuming the entire error budget before the on-call can respond.

questions.question: The four planes of chaos engineering architecture are listed in the lesson. Which of the following is NOT one of the four?
options: Control plane (experiment scheduler)
Safety plane (guards, abort, traffic filters)
Cost plane (budget tracking per experiment)
Observability plane (metrics, traces, logs)
questions.explanation: The four planes are: control (experiment scheduler), target (services, infra, data stores), safety (guards + abort + traffic filters), and observability (metrics + traces + logs). A feedback loop connects observability back into SLO adjustments. Cost tracking is not one of the four planes.

questions.question: Which five LLM-specific chaos experiments does the lesson enumerate?
options: Model version rollback, prompt injection, cold start, token limit exceeded, VRAM OOM
Memory overload, network failures, provider outages, malformed prompts, KV cache eviction storms
Load spike, slow consumer, database latency, DNS failure, certificate expiry
GPU failure, NVLink partition, checkpoint corruption, gradient explosion, weight divergence
questions.explanation: The five LLM-specific experiments: memory overload (force KV eviction), network failures (between prefill/decode pools or to providers), provider outages (simulate API 503), malformed prompts (test guardrails and error handling), and KV cache eviction storms (test preemption handling).

questions.question: What is the recommended chaos engineering cadence from the lesson?
options: Daily small experiments; quarterly game days; annual audits
Weekly small canary experiments; monthly game day + postmortem; quarterly cross-team audit
Monthly experiments only; skip weekly to avoid alert fatigue
Continuous automated experiments; no scheduled game days needed
questions.explanation: The lesson's cadence: weekly small canary experiments in staging (maybe 5% prod); monthly scheduled game days with cross-team attendance and postmortem; quarterly cross-team resilience audits and dependency map updates.

questions.question: How does trace-ID correlation help during chaos experiments?
options: It enables real-time visualization of failure propagation across the service mesh
All experiment-induced errors carry an experiment tag, allowing on-call to deduplicate chaos-induced alerts from real incidents
It connects chaos experiment results to production logs for root cause analysis
It ensures chaos experiments are isolated to a single Kubernetes namespace
questions.explanation: Trace-ID correlation: every request generated by a chaos experiment carries a tag identifying the experiment. On-call engineers can filter these tagged traces out when triaging alerts during an experiment, separating expected chaos-induced errors from unexpected real failures.
